4.2 — Enemy Animation: A Different State Machine

You wired the Player's animator in 1.6, so you already know how animators work: a parameter goes in, a state comes out, and your code never touches a frame of art. Today you meet the enemy's animator — the same API, the same method names, and none of your conventions. Its rules were decided by somebody else and written down nowhere except inside the controller itself. Reading those rules before you write a line is the whole lesson, and it is a skill that will save you in Unit 8.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I read an animator somebody else set up?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

The enemy slides around as a single frozen frame. The art exists, the controller exists, and nothing drives either of them — so "make the enemy animate" is not one problem, it is the job of finding out what somebody else's state machine wants.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Find the Animator somebody else attachedwhat does this part do?Read: the GetComponentInChildren row of this lesson's reference table, and the same line you wrote for the Player in 1.6
  2. Read the contract: the parameter names, their types, and every value they takewhat does this part do?Read: the comparison table above, and the Animator window you learned to read in 1.6
  3. Turn "which way is it moving" into one of those four integerswhat does this part do?Read: the Mathf.Abs line from 1.6 and the SetInteger row of this lesson's reference table
  4. Decide which lifecycle method writes the valuewhat does this part do?Read: the Update and FixedUpdate row of this lesson's reference table, and the lifecycle split from 1.3
  5. Fire the attack, and know what will consume itwhat does this part do?Read: the SetTrigger row of this lesson's reference table, and the mouse-click trigger you wrote in 1.6

Notice the shape: find the machine, read its contract, choose a value, decide when to write it. Three of those four are things you already did in 1.6 for the Player. The new one is that the contract is not yours — in 1.6 you invented the numbers 0, 1 and 2 for WalkDir, and here you inherit four of them from a controller somebody else built. A wrong one is not an error message; it is an enemy that walks the wrong way.

The test for a finished split: does the part name something you could point at? A component, a window, a parameter, a method. "Make the enemy animate" points at nothing; "which object carries the Animator" points at one object on one prefab.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The reference table below names four setters. This controller uses two of them. Say which two, and what each of the other two would cost you if you reached for it out of habit.

This controller has no state the enemy can stand still in. Before you write anything: what do you want the player to see when the enemy stops walking, and is that something your code can produce at all?

In 1.6 you drove an animator you had built yourself: you chose the parameters, you invented the values, and GetComponentInChildren<Animator>() was the line that caught everyone because the Animator sat on the child Sprite. Which part above is that exact line again — and what is different about who decided what the parameters mean?

In 1.6 the attack fired SetTrigger("Attack") on the one frame the mouse button went down, because the held-down version restarted the swing sixty times a second. Which of the enemy's two parameters behaves like that attack, and which behaves like a value that never clears itself?

In 3.1 you looked the player up once in Start() and kept the reference, rather than searching the scene again every frame. Which part above is that same decision — and what is the search looking for this time?

In 1.6 your sideways walk used one clip and spriteRenderer.flipX to mirror it, and your WalkDir had three values. This controller has two separate clips, never flips anything, and has four values. Whose decisions were those, and what do they cost you in code you do not get to write?

The Problem: A Statue That Slides ~20 min

Your enemy patrols, but it slides around as a single frozen frame. The art exists and the animation controller exists — they were simply never connected to any code. Your job is to drive it. But before you write a line, you must find out what the animator wants, and the only place that is written down is the animator itself.

Step 1 — find the Animator. Select the MobileEnemy prefab and look at the child object. Which object carries the Animator component, and which carries the Sprite Renderer? Step 2 — open the Animator window and read the Parameters list. Step 3 — click the states and read every transition's conditions. Write down the exact names, types and numbers before you read any further.

Here is what you should have found, next to what you built yourself in 1.6:

 The Player's animator (you built this)The enemy's animator (already in the project)
Parameters IsWalking (Bool), WalkDir (Int), Attack (Trigger) Direction (Int), Attack (Trigger)
What the Int means 0 = Up, 1 = Horizontal, 2 = Down 0 = Right, 1 = Up, 2 = Left, 3 = Down
Where the Animator lives A child object named Sprite A child object named Sprite
Idle states Yes. Your controller has idle states to fall back on when the player stops. None at all. The controller holds only Walk and Attack states. There is nowhere to go when the enemy stops.
Facing left and right One clip per direction, mirrored with flipX on the Sprite Renderer. Two separate clips — WalkLeft and WalkRight. This controller never touches flipX anywhere.
Attack A Trigger you set from your code. A Trigger you set from your code.
The names look familiar. The numbers do not. Both machines are driven with SetInteger. In yours, 0 means Up; in the enemy's, 0 means Right. A line copied from one script into the other compiles happily and produces an enemy that walks sideways when it should walk up. Two rules follow from this, and they are the point of today:
  • Before you drive any animator, read its parameters and its transitions. Never infer them from the scripts you have already written.
  • An Animator controller is a state machine with its own vocabulary. Two controllers that share an API share nothing else.
The three parameter types, and why Attack is a Trigger.
  • A Bool is a switch. You turn it on and you are responsible for turning it off. Forget the second half and the machine is stuck in that state forever.
  • An Int is a selector. It holds a value indefinitely, so whatever you set last is still true next frame — which is exactly why the enemy controller has no idle state: nothing ever tells it to stop.
  • A Trigger is a one-shot event. It fires once and resets itself, so you cannot forget to clear it. Attacks are events, not conditions — which is why both animators use a Trigger for them.

Socratic: Reading Someone Else's Machine

  1. Your player's WalkDir and the enemy's Direction are both Ints set by SetInteger. Before copying any animator line from one script to the other, what exactly must you check — and where do you check it?
  2. The enemy's controller has no idle states. If your code simply stops calling SetInteger when the enemy stops walking, what does the player see on screen — and is that a bug in your code or a gap in the asset?
  3. Your player mirrors one clip with flipX; the enemy uses two separate clips and never flips. What does the enemy's approach give you that yours cannot — and what does it cost?
  4. Attack is a Trigger, not a Bool. What happens if you model an attack with a Bool and forget to switch it off — and why does a Trigger make that mistake impossible?
  5. Which object on the MobileEnemy prefab carries the Animator, and which GetComponent family call reaches it from the root? What would the plain GetComponent<Animator>() return from the root?
  6. The four Idle clips — IdleUp, IdleDown, IdleLeft, IdleRight — exist as files in the Animations folder. Does their existence mean the enemy has idle states? What is the difference between an asset existing and an asset being wired?
Read the Docs: The API You Already Met ~15 min

This is the level-3 substitute for a walkthrough: the API is laid out below and the code is not. You write the file. Every row here is a call you have made before — in 1.6, on an animator whose rules were yours — and the column that matters today is the last one. Nothing in this table is new; what is new is that the machine on the other end of it was configured by somebody who is not you.

SignatureWhat you getWhat it costs
void SetInteger(string name, int value) The setter you used in 1.6 for the player's WalkDir. Here the parameter is called Direction, and it has four values instead of three. Whatever you set stays set until you set it again. The name is a string, not a keyword: the controller must already have a parameter spelled exactly that way, and a near miss is a Console warning and a frozen sprite rather than a crash. The value is the harder half — 2 is not a direction, it is a number some transition compares against. A wrong value that is still a valid number moves the enemy into the wrong clip in complete silence.
void SetBool(string name, bool value) The setter you used in 1.6 for IsWalking — a value that is true or false and stays that way. Two things. This controller declares no Bool parameter at all, so any name you invent here is a warning and nothing else. And a Bool you set is yours to clear: nothing resets it for you, which is exactly why your player's animation needed a line that set it back to false every frame.
void SetFloat(string name, float value) The fourth member of the family, and the one you have never actually called. It was in 1.6's table for smooth values — a speed, or a point on a walk-to-run blend. It is the wrong tool for a direction. The enemy's controller declares Direction as an Int, and a setter whose type does not match the parameter is a warning and no change: the value never arrives, and nothing on screen tells you so.
void SetTrigger(string name) The one-shot you fired from 1.6's mouse click. No value is passed, because being fired is the whole message, and the animator clears the trigger once a transition has consumed it. It is an event, so it may not be fired every frame — that is 1.6's GetMouseButton mistake in a new costume, where holding the button restarted the swing sixty times a second. And a trigger that no transition is listening for is cleared without doing anything at all, which looks exactly like code that never ran.
T GetComponentInChildren<T>() The lookup from 1.6 that searches the object this script sits on and everything beneath it. It is the one that finds this enemy's Animator, because the Animator is on the child object named Sprite — the same discovery you made on the Player. It searches downwards and takes the first match it meets, so a second Animator anywhere in the children would win without a word. It is also a slower search than the plain version, which is why it belongs in Start() — once — and not in the method that runs every frame.
T GetComponent<T>() The same lookup without the downward search: it looks only at the object this script is attached to. On the enemy root it finds nothing and hands you null, because the Animator is not on the root. That is 1.6's most-repeated bug, and it is nastier here than it looks: the null is created in Start() and used in the frame loop, so the error message points at the line that used it rather than the line that failed.
float Mathf.Abs(float f) The size of a number with the sign thrown away — the comparison you used in 1.6 to work out which axis was being pushed harder, so that walking hard left would not lose to a gentle nudge upward. It throws the sign away, which is exactly what you want in order to choose a direction and exactly what you must not use in order to name one. The losing axis has to be kept raw: on the horizontal axis the sign is the entire difference between the value that means Right and the value that means Left.
void Update() and void FixedUpdate() Update() is the frame loop you have used since 1.4 — once per rendered frame, and where your player's animator has been driven since 1.6. FixedUpdate() runs once per physics step, in step with movement written onto a Rigidbody2D. FixedUpdate() can run twice in one frame or not at all, so a parameter written there can be a rendered frame stale — visible as a half-step of lag on the frame the direction changes. Match the loop to whatever is actually moving the enemy: if the movement came from transform, then Update() is the loop that is in step with it, and the answer is not the same for every enemy you will write.
Five facts the API table cannot carry. A signature tells you how to call something; it cannot tell you what the machine on the other end will do with it. These are the five that decide whether today works, and each one is asked about again below.
  1. A one-shot is forgotten once it has fired; a switch you set yourself is yours to unset. That is the whole difference between a Trigger and a Bool, and it is why an attack may not be fired every frame.
  2. A number means nothing on its own. 0 is a direction only because a transition somewhere compares it to 0 — which is why the same digit means Up in your player's controller and Right in this one.
  3. A component that lives on a child object is reached with a lookup that searches downwards. The object your script sits on and the object that carries the component are not the same object.
  4. Some machines have no stopped state to return to. This controller holds Walk states and Attack states and nothing else, so an enemy that has stopped moving still has a clip playing.
  5. "Stay put" is usually not an instruction — it is the absence of a new one. If your code stops writing Direction, the animator keeps the last value you gave it and keeps animating it.

Each question below opens with one of those five facts, then asks what it means for your enemy. Answer from the table and the callout above, not from the player's script.

Predict Before Building

  1. Example 1 says a cue button is forgotten and a dimmer is not. Which of the enemy's two parameters behaves like the cue button, and which behaves like the dimmer?
  2. Example 2 says the code 0 means something only against the board that defines it. If you paste a line that sets Direction to 2 expecting "Down", what will the enemy actually do? Check the table.
  3. Example 3 reaches a component one level below. Why does the enemy root need the same trick, and what would happen instead of an error if a stray Animator existed on the root?
  4. Example 4 describes a machine with no silent state. Which single fact about the enemy's controller makes the same sentence true of your enemy?
  5. Example 5 says "stay put" is the absence of an instruction. If your code stops giving the enemy instructions, what does the animator keep doing — and why does the answer matter for a guard standing at the end of its beat?
Build Lab: Drive the Enemy's Animator ~25 min

There is no code in this section on purpose. Every call you need is a row in the table above, and every rule you have to obey is written in a window you can open. What is left is the deciding — and the specifications below name the object, the parameter and the question, and stop there.

Step 1 — choose your approach. There is a complete, working script at Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/TopDown_EnemyAnimator.cs. It is not attached to anything. Read it before you decide anything: it is short, it is commented, and it was written by somebody else — which is exactly the skill this lesson is about. Then choose: attach that script, or write your own driver inside EnemyController.cs. Either is defensible. Write down which you picked and why.

Architectural specification: finding the machine.
  • Which object on the MobileEnemy prefab carries the Animator, and which one carries the Sprite Renderer? Check the Inspector rather than assuming it matches the Player.
  • Which GetComponent family call reaches the Animator from the root — and what does the plain version hand back instead: a null, or the wrong component? Name the 1.6 bug you are re-creating.
  • When should that lookup run: once at startup, or every frame? Which of the two did you do for the turret's target in 3.1, and why does the same reasoning apply here?
  • If you chose the package script, which object must you attach it to for its own lookup to succeed? Read its Start() and say what it assumes about the object it sits on — and what it would find if you dropped it on the root instead.
Architectural specification: reading the contract. This is the part that is new today, and it happens before a single line of your own.
  • Open the Animator window on the enemy's controller. How many parameters does it declare, what are their exact names, and what type is each one? Write them down character for character — you are going to type them into strings.
  • Click the transition arrows one at a time. Which parameter does each arrow test, and against which value? You are collecting the mapping from integer to direction, and the controller is the only place it is written down.
  • What does this controller have no state for? How can you answer that by looking at the state graph, without pressing Play at all?
  • Which object carries the Animator, and which controller asset is assigned to it? Where does that asset live in the Project window?
  • Which of your player's conventions does this controller not share — the meaning of the numbers, the number of values, the idle states, the mirroring? List every difference you found in the table above and check you have not missed one.
Architectural specification: turning movement into a number.
  • Which quantity in your enemy's movement tells you which of the four values to write — the movement it was asked for, or the movement that actually happened? Say why, and say which one you can actually read in the method you are writing.
  • The enemy can move on both axes at once, and one axis can be larger than the other. How do you decide which of the four values wins on a diagonal step? Compare the sizes of the two components with Mathf.Abs, the way you did in 1.6, rather than comparing their values — and say why that distinction matters when the enemy is moving left.
  • Write the mapping out in words before you write it in code: which integer is Right, which is Left, which is Up, which is Down. Check every one of them against the Parameters list and the arrows rather than against your memory, and note where your player's numbers differ.
  • Which call actually writes the value — and which member of the Set family matches Direction's declared type? Read the type off the Parameters tab before you choose the setter, and say what the wrong one would do.
  • What value does Direction hold before your code writes anything at all, and what does the sprite do while it sits there?
  • What happens if you write a value that no transition tests? Is that an error you will see, or silence — and which is harder to debug?
Architectural specification: when the value gets written.
  • Which lifecycle method should write the parameter — Update(), which runs once per rendered frame, or FixedUpdate(), which runs once per physics step? What is moving your enemy, and which loop is in step with that?
  • What does the package script use? Read it and find out rather than guessing, then say whether you would have made the same choice and what yours costs.
  • There is no state in this controller for an enemy that has stopped. What do you want the player to see at the end of a beat, and can your code produce it — or is that a gap in the asset you would have to fix inside the controller?
Architectural specification: the attack.
  • Nothing in your enemy attacks yet, so what parameter is waiting for it — and what kind of parameter is it? Which call fires it, and what does that call take?
  • How often may you set it with SetTrigger? Describe what happens on screen if you set it every frame, and name the 1.6 mistake you have just recreated.
  • When 4.3 and 4.4 add pursuit and contact damage, where in that flow will the trigger be set, and what will the Attack states need to line up with?
  • Should the animation decide when damage happens, or should damage decide when the animation plays? Argue a position — this is a real architectural fork and Unit 8 will test it.

Save, play, and watch a full beat. The enemy should face the way it walks, in all four directions, and stop animating only if you work out how to make it stop.

Bug Hunt: Wrong Machine, Wrong Rules

  1. Attach your animation driver to the enemy's root and press Play. What error appears, and which object actually holds the Animator?
  2. Never call SetInteger and simply watch the enemy move. What does the sprite do while Direction sits at its default value?
  3. Set Direction to 4 — a value no state uses. What happens? Why is a wrong-value bug with no error message harder to find than a crash?
  4. Call SetInteger("WalkDir", 1) on the enemy's animator — the parameter name your player uses. What appears in the Console, and what does that prove about parameter names?
  5. Try to face the enemy left by setting flipX on its Sprite Renderer, then walk it left. What do you see, and why does flipX do nothing useful on this rig?
  6. Call SetTrigger("Attack") every frame instead of once. What does the animation do — and which lesson's every-frame problem have you just recreated?
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Change the Rules

  1. The four Idle clips exist in the animations folder but the controller never uses them. What would you have to change — in the controller and in your code — before a standing enemy idles?
  2. Your player animates with one clip and flipX; the enemy uses two clips and never flips. If you had to support eight directions including diagonals, which approach scales better, and what would each one cost you in new animation clips?
  3. Add a Bool parameter to the enemy controller called IsChasing and drive it from your code. If no transition uses it, has anything changed on screen? What is a parameter with nothing attached to it worth?
  4. The package script fires an attack when the mouse button is held. What does that tell you about where it came from, and would you ship it in this game unchanged? Justify your answer in one sentence.
  5. Commit and push: "4.2: enemy animator driven from movement".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name the enemy's two animator parameters and their types, by reading the controller
  • Recite the four Direction values without looking — and say how they differ from your player's
  • Explain why the enemy's animator needs GetComponentInChildren
  • Explain what the enemy does visually when it stops, and why the controller has no answer for it
  • State that this controller uses separate left and right clips and never uses flipX
  • Explain the difference between an animation asset existing and being wired into the controller
  • Break this feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this feature came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
